items.title: When Valid Decisions Are Not Enough: Evaluating Structural Constraints in Knowledge-Guided Generative Systems
items.summary: Knowledge-guided generative systems use explicit domain constraints to improve decision consistency and alignment with human-created solutions. However, locally valid decisions do not necessarily preserve contextual relationships in human decision-making. This paper examines when structural constraints improve or degrade agreement with human reference solutions. We introduce HARMONIX, an experimental framework using automated musical harmonization as a controlled testbed for knowledge-guided decision-making. Four configurations share the same Viterbi-based optimization mechanism: a baseline, repetition constraints, functional constraints, and their combination. Experiments cover 19,745 records and 143,634 motif pairs across training and validation partitions. Combined constraints improve reference root-interval agreement by approximately five percentage points in stable structural contexts but reduce it by nearly nine percentage points in contexts involving transposition tracking. These opposing effects are consistent across both partitions, while overall exact chord agreement changes only marginally. Contexts are identified retrospectively using reference annotations; no adaptive constraint-selection mechanism is evaluated. The findings demonstrate that interpretable constraints can introduce systematic context-specific failures concealed by aggregate accuracy metrics. They highlight the need to evaluate relationships between decisions and the contextual applicability of constraints in knowledge-guided generative systems.

items.title: MT-RGCN-DTI: A Multi-Task Relational Graph Convolutional Network for Drug-Target Interaction Prediction
items.summary: Prediction of drug-target interaction (DTI) has become a very crucial part of drug discovery. With the increase in the data volume, it has become very important to improve prediction accuracy by integrating multiple data sources. In this regard, utilising multiple resources in the form of heterogeneous information network to address DTI prediction can be rewarding. In this work, we propose a heterogeneous information network based multi-task DTI prediction model which leverages the advantages of relation graph convolutional network (RGCN). To achieve this, the model employs drug-target interaction network, drug-drug similarity network and protein-protein similarity network to construct a heterogeneous information network. Moreover, we use a knowledge graph embedding scoring functions to model interactions between drug and targets, specifically DistMult and ComplEx as decoders over the learned node representations. We performed extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets and compared with state-of-the-art methods. We observed that the proposed model shows competitive performance, thereby confirming the effectiveness of our approach. The codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/Dheeran-S/MT-RGCN-DTI/.

items.title: SAFER: Navigating the Exploration-Exploitation Dilemma in World-Model-Based Planning for Autonomous Driving
items.summary: An autonomous vehicle must foresee the consequences of its actions, especially in the rare, time-critical situations where crashes happen. A world model offers this foresight, but only within the coverage of its training data, which poses an exploration-exploitation dilemma. Within this coverage a planner can hardly improve on the data, and beyond it the model's errors mislead it. Logs of competent driving rarely contain the failures that would widen the coverage, and agents that learn from interaction gain them only by failing themselves, without being shown what to do instead. We propose SAFER, a framework that learns offline from failures that others make, judged by an expert, and keeps learning online from its own driving. Offline, partially trained agents and scripted, recoverable perturbations Stage failures in simulation, and an expert Annotates every visited state with its action and value, so that much of what the planner explores is covered before it drives. In planning, a chunked latent world model Foresees the consequences fast enough for real-time use, and a risk-aware sampling-based planner Evaluates candidate maneuvers by their return minus a bounded collision penalty. Online, a loop continuously Refines the model wherever this driving leaves the coverage of the offline data. In closed-loop evaluation against the compared methods, SAFER reaches the highest route completion and reward per step on the CARLA Leaderboard routes, 0.95 and 0.77 from a privileged bird's-eye view, and the highest episode reward in MetaDrive, 53.4 in regular and 49.0 in safety-critical traffic. Project page: https://ys-qu.github.io/safer-website.

items.title: Making Preemption Productive in Long-Output LLM Serving
items.summary: Reasoning LLMs generate long outputs whose key--value (KV) caches occupy GPU memory for minutes. When memory fills, the server preempts requests, and a preempted request can repeatedly lose and recover its state while producing little new output. We call this behavior KV thrashing. In certain cases, existing systems leave more than a fifth of requests stalled for over a minute. Because preemption cannot be avoided without delaying admission, we ask how to make it productive. We present Stint, a serving system that preserves a preempted request's work, bounds how long it waits, and gives it fresh output after it returns. Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in a contiguity-first CPU pool with an exact-extent allocator, and moves them with fused K/V gather/scatter kernels and double buffering. Age-based readmission brings stalled requests back, and protection gives them a turn of fresh decoding before another preemption. Remaining-length estimates from decoding hidden states guide victim selection. On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request pauses for more than 50 seconds under Stint and p99 time per output token falls by 50.7\% relative to recomputation in the same engine. The replay as a whole finishes 10.7\% sooner (12.0\% higher throughput), because the requests that baselines starve no longer finish last.

items.title: Trading Parameters for Accuracy in MambaVision for Chest Radiograph Classification
items.summary: MambaVision, a hybrid state-space and attention backbone, places most of its parameters in its widest, fourth stage. We quantified what that stage contributes to multi-label chest radiograph classification. The fourth stage was replaced with lighter single-scan state-space blocks adapted from Spatial-Mamba, with multi-scale dilated depthwise convolutions applied to the scan output; the first three stages were retained. Tiny, Small, and Base models were evaluated across nine dataset-scale combinations drawn from two source cohorts: the National Institutes of Health ChestX-ray14 archive (full ChestMNIST and a high-resolution subset) and Indiana University Open-i. At the Tiny scale, replacement reduced parameter count by 35.7% and increased graphics processing unit throughput by 19.3%; the savings came from the stage's dense projections, not from removing quadratic attention. Without distillation, the mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve on ChestMNIST was 0.004 lower than the baseline (95% bootstrap confidence interval, 0.002 to 0.006), and 0.003 to 0.006 lower across all nine combinations. Knowledge distillation from an unreplaced teacher narrowed the gap to the undistilled baseline to 0.001-0.002 and met the equivalence criterion on ChestMNIST, but distilling the baseline with the same recipe improved it by 0.001-0.003, so a gap of 0.002-0.005 persisted under symmetric training. At the Base scale, the unreplaced Small model was both smaller and more accurate. Fourth-stage replacement is a useful trade-off only for Tiny and Small models. These measurements let developers of chest radiograph screening tools weigh model size and speed against a quantified loss of diagnostic discrimination.

items.title: EgoSwarm: Learning Decentralized Robot Swarm Intelligence from Human Swarm Demonstrations
items.summary: Advancing from individual embodied intelligence to swarm embodied intelligence is a key step toward scalable, general-purpose embodied intelligence. Complex tasks often require multiple agents to divide responsibilities, coordinate handovers, and manipulate shared objects collaboratively. However, existing robot learning methods rely primarily on individual demonstrations, which provide limited supervision for modeling dependencies among agent actions, while collecting multi-robot demonstrations at scale remains difficult. Human egocentric demonstrations offer a scalable alternative, yet distributed observations from multiple participants cannot directly supervise decentralized policies. We introduce EgoSwarm, the first robot learning framework for learning decentralized multi-robot collaboration from human swarm demonstrations. EgoSwarm collects more than 50 hours of collaborative experience using a robot-free multi-person egocentric system. We introduce the Swarm Interaction Packet (SIP) and Swarm Interaction Token (SIT) to recover cross-agent interaction relations from distributed observations and transform this experience into local supervision consistent with deployment-time information constraints. We further propose SwarmVLA, which transfers knowledge of swarm behavior to decentralized policies conditioned on local observations, local history, and limited neighbor messages. SwarmVLA achieves a mean success rate of 72.2% across three categories of multi-robot collaborative tasks. Project page:https://xitong-c.github.io/EgoSwarm_Page/.

items.title: A Geometric Observer for Visual-Inertial Odometry using Optical-Flow Constraints
items.summary: This paper presents a geometric observer for monocular visual-inertial odometry driven by individual optical-flow constraints. For each tracked point, the bearing and its rotationally compensated derivative give a depth-free homogeneous constraint on the body-frame velocity. These constraints enter the innovation of an observer on the gravity-augmented group $\mathbb{SE}_3(3)$ through a Riccati gain, without estimating depths or reconstructing the direction of motion. The auxiliary gravity state makes the six-dimensional body-frame velocity-gravity error dynamics independent of the attitude correction, and their uniform observability is shown to be equivalent to persistent excitation of a matrix formed from the inertial bearings and their derivatives. Under this condition, the body-frame velocity and gravity errors converge globally and uniformly exponentially, and a gravity-based attitude correction renders the combined velocity, gravity, and reduced-attitude error almost globally asymptotically stable and locally uniformly exponentially stable. Simulations illustrate the excitation condition, recovery from initial errors, and sensitivity to perturbed measurements.

items.title: High-Throughput Serving of Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe with Regime-Aware Megakernels and Kernel Fusion
items.summary: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR leaderboards. Serving it efficiently takes more than fast operators: continuous batching changes the amount and mix of work at every iteration, and the best fusion granularity changes with it. We present a serving engine that, for every pass, chooses between persistent megakernels and chains of fused kernels at crossovers measured offline. On an H100 SXM GPU, throughput of our accuracy-preserving serving peaks at 4,345x real time, 1.39x the peak of tuned vLLM, and is up to 4.39x faster at low concurrency; on B200 it peaks at 6,367x, 1.64x vLLM at the highest concurrency we measured. Word error rate (WER) is 1.91 to 1.93% against 1.88 to 1.93% for vLLM. Within a 400 ms budget for p95 end-to-end completion time, it serves 8x as many concurrent requests. Choosing per pass beats either level alone: 23% higher throughput than always using megakernels at 128 concurrent requests, and 9% higher than always using fused kernels at 8. Opt-in switches, including greedy MoE layer skipping, add 13 to 16% throughput on B200 for offline jobs that can accept higher WER.

items.title: FRAAC: A French Multimodal Large Language Model and Dataset forPictogram-Based Augmentative and Alternative Communication
items.summary: Pictograms are a core modality in augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), yet recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) cannot reliably interpret or produce pictogram sequences. Two obstacles explain this gap: the absence of a standardized pictogram grammar and the scarcity of parallel text-pictogram data. We introduce Retrieval-Augmented Pictogram Selection (RAPS), an annotation method that refines a rule-based transcription system's output with LLM-based concept extraction and retrieval over a pictogram vocabulary, handling cases where hand-written rules fail (named entities, numbers, polysemous words) without requiring new rules. Applied to French, RAPS yields a synthetic corpus of 1.4 million parallel pairs, of which 300k are publicly released. In a human ranking study where annotators order four pictogram transcriptions of the same sentence, RAPS outperforms the rule-based state of the art. Moreover, we show that standard reference-based metrics separate systems of clearly different quality but fail to rank strong systems against each other. Finally, we build an instruction-tuned model that supports interaction in several AAC modalities: it accepts pictogram or text input and answers in pictograms, speech, or text.

items.title: Geo2Gcode: From 3D Geometry to CNC Programs through Structured Machining Primitives
items.summary: Turning a 3D shape into a Computer Numerical Control (CNC) program is still largely manual. For every part, a machinist chooses setups, tools, step-downs, and toolpath patterns. We present Geo2Gcode, which converts a target mesh directly into standard G-code through structured machining primitives. Each primitive couples an indexed machining direction, a closed per-view reconstruction of the target, and explicit tool-radius, layer-height, and clearing-pattern parameters, and compiles deterministically into layerwise toolpaths via signed-distance queries. Most of the fidelity comes from this compiler. A lightweight selector trained with a voxel stock simulator fills in primitive parameters without per-part manual settings, approaching the finest fixed setting at about a quarter of its toolpath length. In simulation on ABC parts, Geo2Gcode reaches roughing fidelity comparable to an expert-tuned commercial CAM setup with a moderately longer toolpath, and clearly improves on a default CAM configuration. Generated programs run in a commercial G-code simulator, and one part is machined on a physical CNC mill. These results demonstrate that roughing programs can be generated directly from geometry without per-part CAM tuning.

items.title: Latent World Modeling for Point-Cloud Video Pretraining
items.summary: Masked modeling is the dominant self-supervised paradigm for point-cloud videos. However, it leaks the information it is meant to predict, whether it reconstructs masked points as in MAE-style methods or predicts their latent features. Because point-cloud tokens are anchored at points sampled from each frame, querying a target at its own position reveals where its geometry has moved, in reconstruction and latent prediction alike. For latent predictors, random spatio-temporal masks introduce a further shortcut, as visible frames on both sides of each target allow interpolation rather than forecasting. The pretext task thus reduces to completion. Once the target positions are withheld, a masked latent predictor performs only slightly better than copying the last frame. To remove this leakage, we propose PointWM, a latent world model that turns completion into forecasting by predicting the features and geometry of future frames from strictly earlier context. Each target is queried only with its last-seen position and timestamp, while a latent action learned without annotations is meant to capture the part of the future that the past leaves undetermined. On HOI4D action segmentation with a P4Transformer backbone, PointWM improves F1@50 over training from scratch by 24.9 offline and 29.1 under strictly causal inference. These results show the promise of latent world models as a leakage-free pretraining paradigm for point-cloud videos.Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/InitalZ/PointWM.

items.title: See the Lives of Stars in a Handful of Light
items.summary: Galaxies evolve over hundreds of millions of years, and no telescope has ever watched one move. Cosmological simulations make this evolution visible as a sequence of multi-view images, inviting the question of whether a galaxy can be recovered in four dimensions from its images. This setting defeats existing dynamic scene methods, since millions of stars span only a few pixels each, faint populations blend into diffuse light, and free deformations reproduce the images without obeying gravity. We present Cosmos4D, which rests on two components. Gravitational 4D Gaussian Splatting represents each star as a self-luminous Gaussian whose motion is integrated through a gravitational potential and a low-dimensional force field shared by all stars. Luminosity-stratified dynamics give bright stars individual orbits supervised across image scales and carry faint populations with a velocity field estimated from optical flow. We further build a 4D dataset of eight galaxies from four cosmological simulations, on which Cosmos4D outperforms dynamic Gaussian baselines in both photometric quality and physical accuracy. With these advancements, we glimpse eight hundred million years of a galaxy's life in ninety-six frames.

items.title: Does Learning Order Explain Forgetting? The Lie Bracket as an Early-Warning Signal for Catastrophic Forgetting Without Old Data
items.summary: A network trained on task A and then task B ends at different weights than one trained on B and then A. To leading order this gap is set by the Lie bracket of the two tasks' gradient fields, and Dherin (2023) conjectured that a non-vanishing bracket may be linked to catastrophic forgetting. I test this conjecture empirically. Across Split MNIST, Split Fashion-MNIST and Split CIFAR-10, the forgetting of A is almost exactly the difference in A's loss between the two training orders (Spearman rho = 0.96-1.00). I then ask whether the bracket can predict that forgetting early in training on B and without any of A's data, using only a small summary stored when A finishes: its gradient and its top 20 Hessian eigenpairs. When the old task is well learned and forgetting is slow (task-incremental), this stored bracket ranks forgetting with rho = 0.70-0.81, against 0.33-0.58 for the penalty of Elastic Weight Consolidation, and matches or exceeds re-evaluating A on its own data. When forgetting is fast (domain-incremental), the stored summary goes stale and the EWC penalty is as good or better. The bracket fails outright when the old task is only half learned; I trace this to a residual gradient on A an order of magnitude larger, which makes first-order (slope) damage matter. The bracket is therefore a useful early-warning signal for the quiet kind of forgetting, under a clear condition.

items.title: Infrastructure-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Attention for Highway Ramp Merging
items.summary: On-ramp merging is a typical safety and throughput problem on highways. Without proper coordination, human drivers and self-interested autonomous vehicles may make risky manoeuvres and cause accidents or congestion. With recent advances in connected autonomous vehicles (CAVs) and multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), vehicles can be trained to coordinate for safe and efficient merging. However, in dense traffic, forming an effective observation of the traffic state is challenging. For example, observing only the neighbouring vehicles may lead to locally optimal decisions, while observing the entire traffic can introduce much irrelevant information. In this paper, we propose a transformer-based MARL vehicle control model to address these problems. A roadside infrastructure controller receives the states of all CAVs via vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) communication and sends control commands back to them. An attention-based observation encoder is designed where each vehicle can filter the relevant vehicle information from the global traffic state. The proposed model is evaluated in SUMO against three baselines: a model that observes only the neighbouring vehicles, a model that encodes the global traffic information, and the rule-based SUMO model. The results show that our model achieves the highest traffic flow, safety and smoothness. Furthermore, in a four-hour simulation with dynamic traffic demand, our model successfully avoids traffic jams, while other baseline models fail at high traffic flow. We also show that our model remains effective when human-driven vehicles are present. We further show that our model, trained in ideal communication conditions, can still remain collision-free and maintain throughput under realistic V2I communication errors. Finally, we visualise the relevance weights that an ego vehicle assigns to other vehicles in multiple traffic situations.

items.title: SGIP: Learning Scene-Grounded Interaction Priors for Scene-Aware Human Motion Prediction
items.summary: Human motion prediction (HMP) aims to forecast future movement from an observed motion sequence, and recent methods have incorporated 3D scene geometry and object semantics to improve long-term plausibility. However, the destination of future motion remains ambiguous in cluttered scenes: the same observed motion can lead to different interaction targets or navigation modes. Existing methods either handle this ambiguity implicitly or rely on auxiliary signals like gaze that are hard to obtain in practice. To address this, we propose SGIP, which explicitly predicts where in the scene future motion will be grounded across both objects and open navigation regions, and uses it to condition future trajectory and full-body pose prediction. This scene-grounded interaction prior is learned via intent distillation: at training time only, a teacher model scores candidate scene regions by combining an LLM prompted with a textual description of the person's intent with geometric motion-scene features. A student model learns to reproduce these scores from only the observed motion and 3D scene, making intent and LLM unnecessary at test time. Across multiple benchmark datasets, SGIP outperforms prior scene-aware baselines on both trajectory and pose accuracy in a realistic deployment setting where neither gaze nor intent is available at inference, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework. The project page is available at https://sgip2026.github.io.

items.title: Prompt Re-Specification and Target-Mask Availability in Mask-Conditioned Visual Reinforcement Learning for Moving-Platform Landing
items.summary: Visual reinforcement learning (RL) policies that land a drone on a moving platform can fail when the landing pad looks different from the one used in training. Using binary target masks as the visual input removes most pixel-level appearance information while preserving the spatial representation of the target, and lets a text prompt specify the target. In simulation, we test whether a frozen (fixed-weight) mask-based DrQ-v2 policy can handle a new pad when only the prompt of its fine-tuned SAM 3 detector changes. A banana-themed pad lowered landing success from 75.6% to 12.0%, and SAM 3 rarely detected it under the original prompt. A revised prompt, chosen after testing several candidates, restored success to 68.4% with no weight updates. In a separate experiment with a policy trained on ground-truth masks, filling in masks that were missing while the pad was visible helped landing far more than the tested mask-centroid and area corrections. Tracking the pad over time supplied masks more often and also kept producing them after the pad was confirmed absent from the rendered image, but it did not establish a reliable improvement in landing success. Whether a usable mask reaches the policy at all thus appears to be an important limiting factor for this approach.

items.title: The Silent Cost of Conversation History in LLM Reasoning
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) in multi-turn information systems accumulate their own earlier replies and a growing task state. We asked whether this conversation history lowers accuracy, and whether process-level quality metrics warn before it does. Each analysis was fixed before its outcomes were computed. In Study 1, on 48 sharded math tasks, retaining its replies lowered final success by 0.21 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.29 for Mistral-7B (Holm-adjusted p = 0.026 and 0.004); Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction, not significant. Study 2 introduces CDR-Stream, 100-turn state-tracking dialogues with an exact answer per turn and per-model difficulty calibration. With the full history, accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within twenty turns at matched difficulty, whereas a solver-verified state summary kept it 0.52-0.59 higher (Holm-adjusted p less than 0.001). Consistency and logical coherence fell far less than accuracy, and stability rose. None of these metrics, a paired readiness measure or calibrated single-stream drift detectors gave robust, model-general early warning, although in Study 2 the repeat-based metrics were complete only for GPT-4o-mini. In the monitors we tested, a single 100-turn stream had power only for very large drops. Systems built on LLMs should keep task state outside the transcript and monitor across sessions.

items.title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Lookup Table Demappers for Amplitude Phase-Shift Keying over Nonlinear Satellite Links
items.summary: Next-generation high-throughput satellites increasingly demodulate and decode on board, so the per-symbol cost of the receiver constrains payload power and throughput. Soft demappers for nonlinear satellite links must therefore produce accurate bit log-likelihood ratios (LLRs) at low cost. We introduce a KAN-LUT demapper, a two-layer Kolmogorov--Arnold network (KAN) whose learned univariate edge functions are stored as 128-entry lookup tables (LUTs), so that inference needs only table reads, linear interpolation, and additions. We bound the LLR error introduced by the tables and evaluate the demapper on amplitude phase-shift keying (APSK) links with low-density parity-check (LDPC) coding and a nonlinear traveling-wave-tube amplifier. For 16-, 32-, and 64-APSK, KAN-LUT stays within 0.2 dB of a per-cluster Gaussian log-MAP (LogMAP-CG) demapper, while its cost relative to LogMAP-CG falls from 87% to 27% as the order grows. It matches or slightly exceeds multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) at about one fifth of their cost, remains competitive under operating-point mismatch, and needs only tens of kilobytes of tables. KAN-LUT is therefore a low-cost candidate demapper for regenerative payloads.

items.title: MARLIN: Multiscale And Directional Sparse Representation Learning for Imbalanced SAR Ship Classification
items.summary: Despite recent progress in SAR maritime monitoring, ship classification remains challenging due to limited labeled data, class imbalance, large intra-class variability, fine-grained inter-class similarity, and variations in target scale, orientation, and backscattering structure. To address these challenges, this paper proposes MARLIN, a class-frequency-aware framework with directional sparse and hierarchical multi-scale feature extraction for ship type classification in SAR images. The proposed architecture first constructs two complementary representations of each input image, where each views are processed by parallel encoder branches. Each branch begins with a directional sparse convolutional stem designed to capture elongated and orientation-dependent ship scattering patterns, followed by customized hierarchical multiscale feature extraction blocks. To improve learning under imbalanced class distributions, we introduce a class-frequency aware objective. The proposed objective combines margin-based classification with class-frequency-weighted prototype compactness and class-pair frequency weighted margin separation. This formulation shapes the embedding space by encouraging samples from the same class to form compact clusters while enforcing stronger separation for class pairs involving underrepresented ship categories. Extensive experiments on three complementary datasets demonstrate that in addition to being lightweight and parameter efficient, MARLIN improves both overall accuracy and class-balanced metrics, confirming its effectiveness for robust SAR ship-type classification under limited and imbalanced training conditions. The codes are available at github.com/benyaminhosseiny/marlin.

items.title: Decode Early, Verify Late: Streaming Offline Speech Recognizers Without Accuracy Loss
items.summary: Voice agents need accurate transcripts soon after a user stops speaking. We propose Decode Early, Verify Late (DEVL), a training-free framework for streaming inference with offline ASR models. The server keeps partial transcripts as drafts and verifies the latest against the complete audio in one forward pass at turn end. Under stated input and decoding conditions, the final equals the model's greedy offline output in exact arithmetic. We adapt DEVL to four model families. In our five-recognizer comparison, 95-100% of final transcripts are byte-identical to the offline transcripts, WER stays within 0.13 points of offline, and single-stream time to final falls 1.5-7.3x. Serving Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on one A100, DEVL returns finals a median 22-26 ms after turn end at up to 64 streams, 2.7-3.9x sooner than the official streaming mode. It is the only system we tested that meets a 100 ms p99 target, up to 80 streams on Pipecat-STT and 64 on WildASR.

items.title: Mandarin Wh-Indefinites Follow Nonveridicality in Multilingual LLMs, Unlike English any
items.summary: Multilingual LLMs learn mostly from English. Do they carry English polarity licensing over to other languages? English any is licensed by downward-entailing (DE) contexts, Mandarin wh-indefinites such as shenme 'what/something' by nonveridical ones, and the two classes come apart: perhaps licenses shenme but not any, while only licenses any but entails existence. We test this dissociation in a pre-registered study of twelve open LLMs (0.5B-9B, four families), using 48 matched bilingual frames in 21 contexts and a log-probability difference-in-differences normalised by negation. All 11 models that pass the measurement gate license Mandarin wh-indefinites under possibility, necessity and evidential adverbs, at 0.42-2.33 times the strength of negation, while English any gets nothing in the same contexts. An exploratory extension to Qwen2.5-32B shows the same. The English side is weaker: any under only, first and regret is licensed but at a fraction of negation, so only 3 models show the full double dissociation in sentence probabilities. When prompted to choose between sentences, most gated models show it. In exploratory directional ablations, a direction that carries English licensing, held-out classes included, does not reach Mandarin licensing in most models. The models do not simply apply the English rule to Mandarin.

items.title: Communication-Efficient Distributionally Robust Federated Averaging with Multi-Source Data
items.summary: Federated learning trains a shared model from distributed client data. The deployment risk is typically specified through two approximations: each unknown local distribution is replaced by its empirical distribution, and the unknown deployment mixture across clients is replaced by empirical or prescribed training weights. Existing robust methods usually address one approximation at a time through local distributional ambiguity sets or worst-case client mixtures. However, joint treatment of both approximations remains underexplored. To address this gap, we construct a global ambiguity set formed by admissible mixtures of client-wise Wasserstein ambiguity sets, yielding a distributionally robust optimization formulation. The construction allows client-dependent ambiguity radii, preserves client-wise separability of the objective function, and yields a high-probability out-of-sample guarantee for the resulting robust problem. We then introduce a penalty-based approximation of this formulation and develop a communication-efficient algorithm called BiDRO-FedAvg, for which we establish a convergence guarantee. We validate the proposed framework through a market-demand prediction simulation.

items.title: SWAN-Rx: Efficient and Bandwidth-Scalable Neural Reception for MIMO-OFDM
items.summary: We present a Scalable Windowed Axial-attention Neural Receiver (SWAN-Rx) for multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) systems. The receiver improves reception accuracy and reduces forward-pass computation while supporting frozen-weight reuse across bandwidth allocations and channel conditions. It combines a common resource-element representation of received observations and pilot context with alternating time-axis and local frequency-axis attention. Shared parameters and relative positional information permit soft detection across allocation lengths without inference-time parameter updates. At fixed subcarrier spacing, model configuration, and symbol count, bounded frequency neighborhoods give linear growth of forward-pass computation with bandwidth. Evaluations compatible with the 5G New Radio physical layer reuse weights trained on four physical resource blocks (PRBs) at up to 273 PRBs and on unseen channels. At the training bandwidth, SWAN-Rx achieves lower pre- and post-decoding bit error rates than the implemented three-step neural receiver (NRX) and DeepRx-MIMO baselines, with 16.9% and 39.7% fewer parameters and 56.3% and 35.7% fewer forward-pass operations, respectively. The same weights achieve lower pre-decoding error rates than these baselines throughout the evaluated bandwidth-extrapolation and 16-PRB channel-transfer tests, with an estimated 0.4-0.9 dB signal-to-noise ratio reduction relative to NRX at a pre-decoding error rate of $10^{-2}$ in the 16-PRB tests.

items.title: Clinician Assessment of Laryngeal Disease with Auditory AI before Laryngoscopy: A Paired Reader Study
items.summary: Background: Before laryngoscopy, clinicians assess the likely cause of hoarseness and whether to suspect a precancerous or malignant lesion. Whether voice-based artificial intelligence (AI) supports pre-laryngoscopic categorization is unknown. Methods: We developed an auditory large language model that generates a patient-level assessment card (provisional category, voice-quality ratings, and rationale) and a prespecified malignancy alert from voice recordings, patient information, and acoustic measures obtained before laryngoscopy at one center. We evaluated both in a held-out test set and a later cohort. In a sequential reader study, 32 otolaryngology clinicians categorized held-out cases without AI and, 1 to 2 weeks later, reviewed their initial categories with the card (without the alert). Results: Across 800 paired assessments, reader accuracy was 49.8% before and 56.8% after review (difference, 7.0 percentage points; 95% CI, 1.7 to 13.5; P < 0.001); 99 categories changed from incorrect to correct and 43 from correct to incorrect (ratio, 2.30; 95% CI, 1.22 to 5.31). Accuracy rose 14.7 points when the model was correct and fell 8.7 when incorrect. Provisional-category accuracy was 72% in held-out testing and 67% in temporal validation. The malignancy alert flagged 85.7% and 86.8% of precancerous or malignant lesions. Sensitivity for precancerous or malignant lesions increased from 53.9% to 75.0% after AI-assisted review (difference, 21.1 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.3 to 42.0). Conclusions: In this single-center study, clinicians' pre-laryngoscopic categorization accuracy was higher after reviewing the AI assessment card, although the sequential design cannot fully separate AI assistance from reassessment; gains depended on model correctness without clearly selective adoption. Randomized and external evaluations, including of the malignancy alert, are needed.

items.title: The Frontier Must Grow - Self-proposed, interpreter-labelled training roughly doubles a 4B model's accuracy on a fresh exam as its verified frontier grows
items.summary: A model can learn from problems it poses itself when an executable oracle supplies the answers. Qwen3-4B proposed Lua 5.1 programs; those it predicted wrong at least once in four samples joined a pool labelled by the interpreter, each round adding twice as many programs as the last (300, 900, 2100 in total), and each round trained a fresh adapter from the base on the pool. On the original exam the procedure met its registered criterion, an item-level test of each adapter against its predecessor. On a 2340-item exam drawn afterwards, accuracy rose from 8.3% to 16.7%; that follow-up's registered criteria were not met because round 1 gained nothing, while rounds 2 and 3 added 5.0 and 2.9 points on average, both intervals above zero. One fit on the same amount of base-proposed frontier data reached 14.6%, so the rounds' 2.1-point advantage is inconclusive. Three earlier registered series met no per-lineage criterion, and the same loop showed no gain on repository tasks or for a 27B agent in those configurations.

items.title: Security of Deep Research Agents: Attack Surface, Defenses, Benchmarks, and Agenda Seeding against Research Planning
items.summary: Deep research and agentic search agents autonomously retrieve content from the open web and generate reports with citations, and their outputs are often taken directly as research conclusions. This paper systematizes security research in this area along four stages, namely retrieval, planning, evidence integration, and report generation. We present a unified threat model, a taxonomy of attacks and defenses, and a review of evaluation benchmarks, and we align the area dimension by dimension with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) poisoning, prompt injection, and generative engine optimization (GEO). Coding 34 primary studies shows that only 26.5% of them involve the planning stage, and none performs an end-to-end poisoning evaluation on commercial products. To address this gap, we propose the agenda seeding attack, in which the attacker writes no instructions and only introduces a fictitious evaluation metric. Across 3,520 sandboxed research runs under the same budget, GEO and prompt injection are nearly ineffective, whereas agenda seeding makes the attacker's target the top pick in 16% to 28% of reports. Injection detection and query anchoring fail against it, verification prompting hurts utility, and our proposed provenance tagging preserves utility but can be bypassed by multi-site bait. Finally, we propose eight research directions.

items.title: A Dataset for Misogyny Detection in Polish Social Media: Transferability of Hateful Speech Detection from General to Specific Types of Hate
items.summary: Harmful language detection is commonly evaluated on broadly defined hate speech and toxicity benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether models that successfully detect harmful language in general can transfer this capability to more specific forms of hate. We investigate this problem for misogyny detection in Polish, an area for which dedicated resources remain scarce. We introduce a new dataset of Polish social media comments annotated for misogyny, gender-directed hateful speech. Using this resource, we first assess the reliability of LLM-assisted annotation and then evaluate general-to-specific transfer by comparing models trained on general harmful language data, safety-specialized models, and models fine-tuned directly for misogyny detection. Our results show that strong performance on general harmful language detection does not transfer uniformly to misogyny; safety-specialized models demonstrate substantially stronger generalization ability. The study contributes a new Polish resource for gender-directed harmful language and demonstrates that the scope and granularity of prior safety training are important factors in transferring harmful language detection from general to specific forms of hate.

items.title: Machine Learning for Near Real-Time Identification of Wildfire Burned Areas
items.summary: In this article, we present a near real-time method that estimates burned probability anywhere in the world using satellite images. Our approach takes advantage of the state-of-the-art pix2pix model to translate a preprocessed index calculated from Landsat 8/9 images into an approximate of USGS Burn Probability indicating per pixel burn probability. Since this is a machine learning-based approach, it can be automated with a minimum amount of human intervention with significantly less time delays and geographic restrictions compared to other contemporary methods. We include results from our experiments and compare our approximation with the USGS Burn Probability using RMSE score.

items.title: U-HamGNN: a universal model for magnetic Hamiltonians conditioned on spin and Hubbard U
items.summary: The electronic structure of a magnetic crystal depends jointly on its spin configuration and the on-site Hubbard correction U, requiring a separate DFT+U calculation for each combination. We introduce U-HamGNN, an equivariant network that takes these two inputs directly and predicts spin-resolved Hamiltonians across diverse crystal chemistries. A spectral-hybrid optimizer that weights each update direction by how consistently the gradient points along it reaches 8% lower Hamiltonian error than Muon and 26% lower than AdamW in a ten-epoch benchmark. The predicted bands reproduce U-dependent gap opening and altermagnetic spin splitting within the trained window and beyond it; exchange couplings and magnetic-order calls derived from the Hamiltonian agree with DFT+U on a calibration set. This universal model provides a new tool for magnetic research.

items.title: Towards Agentic Scientific Discovery in Distributed Systems
items.summary: We investigate when adaptive tool selection helps identify a shared equation across clients with different input coverage. Query-ATLAS (query-conditioned Agentic Tool-based Learning for Aggregating Symbolic Equations) uses an LLM to guide symbolic search from client errors and previous proposals in a simulated distributed system. A four-architecture comparison reveals task-dependent opportunities: relative to fixed PySR-LLM, validation acceptances rise from 3/12 to 7/12 on CRK3 and from 11/12 to 12/12 on oscillator2, while MatSci3 favors the fixed workflow. Across 72 settings in a post-hoc six-task subset of eight development tasks, Query-ATLAS achieves 64 validation and 64 in-distribution passes, versus 62 and 59 for the fixed workflow; both pass 47/60 eligible out-of-distribution tests. The fixed workflow retains lower median errors and cost. Broader query coverage emerges as a promising benefit, motivating task-aware tool selection and client-aware fitting for scientific agents.

items.title: acuSimNet: Multi-View Self-Occlusion-Awared Visibility Learning for Cranio-Cervical Acupuncture Points
items.summary: The localization of acupuncture points (acupoints) in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) presents unique challenges since they are defined by abstract principles rather than distinct anatomical landmarks. Existing approaches are typically constrained to single view or rely on indirect calculations of relative positions with respect to other landmarks, thereby overlooking human anatomical variations. Furthermore, acupoint visibility assessment, which determins whether points are occluded by human itself, hair, clothing, or other objects, has received limited attention in practical applications. Acupoint localization itself does not require 3D reconstruction, but inferring their occlusion relationships with anatomical surfaces does, which adds computational cost and limits real-time inference. In this work, we introduce acuSimNet, an efficient hierarchical multi-task learning architecture for multi-view, self-occlusion-aware visibility prediction of acupoints, achieving 99.97% accuracy on the validation set. Our approach also addresses the challenges of high-dimensional classification (174 acupoints in cervicocranial region), negative convergence issues for visible acupoints, and inter-task scheduling optimization, resulting in substantially accelerated convergence. We improved the training efficiency from the exisiting methods of 3000 epochs to achieve 99% validation accuracy, to our optimized framework achieving 90% accuracy in 39 epochs and 99% accuracy in 86 epochs. This architecture overcomes the limitations of existing methods, could enable practical applications in acupoints detection and visualization, advancing the automation of TCM.

items.title: FastGRN: Few-Step Generative Refinement Networks
items.summary: Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) generate an image by repeatedly re-predicting and refining every token of a discrete latent. They reach high fidelity, but need dozens of Markov steps. We therefore train few-step GRNs on the distribution of their own samples. We use its own uniform-state corruption to perform distribution matching on discrete tokens, which lets a discrete generator learn by backpropagation, and we pair noise with samples in the manner of rectified flow. We find that the steps of a few-step GRN do not carry the same amount of information or the same repair load. We therefore exploit its discrete refinement during training and build few-step GRNs in three parts. Oversampling samples the student with more steps than it was trained for and refines its judge on these samples. Non-uniform sampling trains only the last step and hands it most of the information at sampling time. Refinement confidence keeping holds on to the tokens the student is already sure of. We train a fast class-conditional generator on ImageNet 256 and, with the same method, a 2B text-to-image model. On ImageNet 256, the 3-step FastGRN beats the FID of GRN. On a 2B binary-token text-to-image GRN, a 4-step student also nearly matches the GenEval of GRN-T2I 2B.

items.title: Improving fine-grained expressivity of graph neural networks
items.summary: This thesis investigates the expressive power of neural networks for structured data, focusing on graph neural networks and symmetry-aware architectures. We present four main contributions. First, we characterize the generic expressive power of geometric message-passing neural networks on sparse graphs and introduce EGenNet, an architecture achieving the corresponding guarantees. Second, we use representation theory to characterize linear layers equivariant to multiple permutations, including wreath-product symmetries. Third, we study permutation-invariant set representations that preserve containment, establish dimensional bounds and impossibility results, and introduce MASNet. Finally, we propose FSW-GNN, a message-passing architecture combining strong expressivity and bi-Lipschitz stability guarantees with strong empirical performance on long-range graph-learning tasks. Together, these results provide a broader understanding of how neural architectures can preserve the geometric, algebraic, order-theoretic, and metric structure of their inputs.

items.title: D'BEAST: Logged Bad Experiences as Explanation for Autonomous Driving Agents
items.summary: Reinforcement learning agents learn from mistakes, yet their decisions can be difficult to trace back to those experiences. We investigate whether a tabular agent's decisions can be explained by its bad experiences, defined as the training transitions associated with safety or task events. A fixed training log is replayed from the same initial Q-table under three conditions. FULL retains all updates, SKIP omits bad-experience updates, and NEUTRALIZE retains those updates without their event penalties. We illustrate the method on six classic Markov decision processes and evaluate it in closed-loop driving in CARLA. On the full driving task, FULL reached the goal from 33 of 40 test starts, whereas SKIP and NEUTRALIZE reached it from none, indicating that the bad experiences carry decision-relevant information. At the local level, for 47 decisions shortly before a failure of SKIP or NEUTRALIZE, removing or neutralizing a small group of bad experiences, with a median size of one, caused the trained agent to select the failing policy's action in 46 cases. For this agent, the results indicate that its decisions can be explained by its bad experiences.

items.title: GEM-MM: Reducing VLM Hallucination with Entropy-Guided Preference Alignment
items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are routinely aligned with offline pairwise RLHF objectives, but multimodal preference data is scarce and treats every response token as equally informative. Under a small preference budget, pair construction becomes nearly irrelevant: standard DPO-style, image-conditional, and self-improvement objectives all perform within 1.1 points on MM-RLHF metrics and 0.5 points on hallucination rates, matching the SFT baseline. We call this entropy-blind preference optimization: the learning signal ignores policy uncertainty, which in chain-of-thought VLMs concentrates on specific fork tokens where visual claims are made. We introduce GEM-MM, extending entropy-guided preference modeling to VLMs. It samples on-policy candidates, rewards high-entropy reasoning forks, penalizes uncertain final answers, and updates the model via group-normalized policy gradients. On a 3000-prompt MM-RLHF budget with Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, GEM-MM achieves the best entropy-depth preference score (61.7% vs. 57.3-58.4% baselines) and implicit-reward accuracy (41.4%). Crucially, it reduces AMBER hallucination from 23.4-24.0 to 20.6 and CHAIR from 5.0-5.1 to 4.6 at matched caption coverage. It also ranks best on all three HallusionBench granularities, with a conservative operating point raising the near-chosen rate to 62.4%. An off-the-shelf multimodal reward model ranks GEM-MM first, and two such models independently confirm our main ablations (p < 0.001). We report confidence intervals, paired significance tests, metric-reward functional overlaps, and document a collapse mode when exceeding the fair budget. Code and evaluation harness: https://github.com/SNOWTEAM2023/GEM-MM

items.title: Offline-First Quantized AI: Design and Evaluation of an On-Device Maternal-Health Assistant for Low-Connectivity Environments
items.summary: Offline language models could extend access to maternal-health information where internet connectivity is unreliable, but deployment requires both clinically appropriate responses and feasible local execution. This study presents an offline Android assistant integrating ready-made quantized language models, a clinically validated local knowledge package, conversational context, and model-initiated local retrieval. Gemma 4 E2B and Qwen3.5 0.8B were compared across 45 conversations and 312 turns per configuration, including a dedicated offline agentic benchmark. Gemma achieved higher response-quality, context-retention, and safety scores; Qwen offered faster generation and lower memory use. Clinician assessment of 150 Gemma responses across nine clinical domains yielded a mean quality score of 3.80/4, with 147 responses meeting the acceptance criterion. A paired RAG-on/off experiment evaluated 74 questions: retrieval improved 11 responses, left 56 neutral, produced four adverse response changes, and left three pairs unassessable. RAG-on had descriptively higher mean usefulness, safety, correctness, and actionability in the conditional 70-pair subset excluding the four flagged pairs from both conditions. Physical-device testing demonstrated offline responses on a 6 GB Android handset, with a 14.3 s median latency, alongside successful reconnection synchronization in the integrated application. Together, the findings document clinical response quality and practical performance of the integrated offline maternal-health assistant.

items.title: ReactBench-AD: Do Driving VLAs and World-Action Models React to Imminent Hazards in Their Path?
items.summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged in autonomous driving with the promise of strong generalization to long-tail scenarios. Although these models achieve state-of-the-art results on autonomous driving benchmarks, most existing benchmarks are dominated by nominal scenarios and therefore cannot test this promise. To test one such long-tail capability that is critical for safety, we introduce ReactBench-AD, a benchmark that measures how driving models react to objects that appear in the ego vehicle's path. Built on real NAVSIM and PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles scenes, ReactBench-AD composites a crossing pedestrian, a standing pedestrian, or a stationary car consistently across all camera views and history frames. Each edited scene thus forms an exact, pixel-level counterfactual pair with its original, which allows us to isolate the causal effect of the inserted object on the predicted trajectory. Evaluating four VLAs and two WAMs, we find that they react weakly, often barely at all. Finally, we test how easily one of the evaluated VLAs, ReCogDrive, can be taught to brake hard for imminent hazards: a short fine-tuning stage on edited scenes substantially improves its reactions, with the learned behavior generalizing to unseen objects and fully real scenes, at minimal cost to nominal driving. These results call into question the out-of-the-box long-tail capabilities of these models, but suggest that they can be a strong foundation for acquiring them with little additional training, highlighting the value of real or synthetic data that demonstrates the long-tail behaviors nominal datasets rarely contain. Code and data will be made publicly available.

items.title: PlanDiv: Test-Time Scaling with Latent Plans for Vision-Language-Action Models
items.summary: Test-time scaling improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies by drawing several action candidates and executing the best one. We find that its returns diminish quickly when the candidates are resampled from one decoder: they differ by noise rather than by plan, and for each of three resampling sources, going from four to eight candidates adds only 0.06-0.07 to the average number of completed tasks on CALVIN. We introduce PlanDiv, an action head that makes the candidates differ by plan: a lightweight planner proposes K latent plan hypotheses, a shared masked-diffusion executor decodes one action chunk per plan from a single backbone pass, and the policy executes the chunk that its own likelihood ranks highest. The plans are learned from demonstrations alone, without plan labels or rewards. With the backbone, data and training recipe held fixed, eight plan-conditioned candidates raise five-task chain success on CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D from 56.9% to 69.9%, while eight candidates from autoregressive, plan-free or same-plan resampling reach at most 64.9%. The same-plan baseline is PlanDiv's own checkpoint with the plan held fixed, so this gap comes from the plans, not from drawing more samples. On LIBERO-Long, four plans remove 40% of single-candidate failures, against at most 21% for matched resampling. On a real Franka arm the gain appears where a task admits more than one solution: PlanDiv is on par with a single-output OpenVLA-OFT+ baseline on a one-solution task and succeeds in 51 of 54 trials against 40 of 54 on two tasks with two solutions.

items.title: Glance, then Select: Evidence-Tempered Visual Token Selection for Extremely Compressed Multimodal LLMs
items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) encode a high-resolution image into thousands of visual tokens, which dominate the cost of the prefill stage. Visual token reduction removes most of these tokens, but two problems remain at extreme budgets. The vision encoder still processes every patch of the image, and the few surviving tokens often miss the small regions that hold the answer. In this paper, we propose Glance-ETD, a two-stage token reduction framework guided by a lightweight question-conditioned scorer. In the first stage, a glance encoder views the image at low resolution and re-encodes only the question-relevant regions at native resolution. In the second stage, Evidence-Tempered Diversity (ETD) selects the final tokens by combining diversity with the evidence predicted by the scorer, so that the kept tokens cover the scene and retain the answer. A single-rollout self-distillation recipe trains the MLLM with the glance encoder. With only 5% of the visual tokens, Glance-ETD retains 91.6% of the full-token performance of Qwen3.5-4B across fourteen benchmarks and outperforms the strongest prior method, LT-OPD, by 17.3 points and the same training recipe with DivPrune by 6.0. It also speeds up the time to first token on 4K images by 3.1x and generalizes to three other MLLMs and to high-resolution document benchmarks, with the largest gains on text-rich tasks.

items.title: The novelty exposed: ablation, reproducibility and transparency in 40 technical reports of open-weight large language models (LLMs)
items.summary: In 2025 alone, 48 new large language model (LLM) architectures were added to the Hugging Face transformers library, and many of them arrive with a technical report that presents the model as new. What is actually new in these models, and is it tested? We put this question to LLM technical reports. We look at three things: what the reference code shows about how new open-weight architectures differ from earlier ones; what 40 randomly sampled technical reports claim as new and whether they support it with ablation studies; and what they disclose for reproducibility and transparency. In the library, 39 of the 48 architectures added in 2025 take at least two of their three core blocks from another model, most often Llama, although part of this reflects how the library writes code. In the reports, 19 of 73 architectural or training novelty claims come with a controlled with/without comparison; 4 of 40 reports state more than one training run; 8 rerun the models they compare against under one setup; and 1 discloses data mixture, token count, and compute together. We also looked for known components given new names: none of five candidate cases hid its origin, though we did not study model names. We propose seven reporting rules for LLM release reports and apply them to two reports. We do not judge model quality, and an untested claim may still be true.

items.title: What Matters for Cross-Modal Alignment
items.summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that models trained on different modalities converge toward a shared representation. Related work aligns frozen image and text encoders on natural images without paired data. We test zero-pair alignment on five datasets across four modalities: natural images, environmental audio, chest radiographs, and 3D computed tomography (CT). It succeeds only on COCO and fails on the other four. We analyze the failures and find that alignment must first locate the subspace where the modalities co-vary and then orient the mapping within it. Consistent with previous studies, medical imaging is the hardest case: its shared subspace carries the smallest fraction of the variance. When this fraction is small, alignment needs image-text pairs, and random-matrix theory predicts how many pairs are needed. These findings motivate LightAlign: a few pairs let a ridge regression between two frozen encoders locate and orient the mapping simultaneously, and a classifier fitted only on report text then predicts findings from the mapped images. On 3D CT, LightAlign surpasses models trained end to end on image-report pairs without finding-level labels: with only 200 pairs, LightAlign outperforms CT-CLIP on CT-RATE (0.754 vs. 0.733 AUROC), and with only 100 CT-RATE pairs, it does so on RAD-ChestCT, an out-of-distribution dataset from a different hospital. On CheXpert, it reaches 0.862 mean AUROC with only about 5% as many pairs as models trained on MIMIC-CXR.

items.title: Back to Pixels: Lifting Latent Video Diffusion into Pixel Space
items.summary: Frontier video generation models work in a VAE latent space that compresses video in both space and time. This compression made training tractable, but now limits high-resolution, controllable, and interactive generation -- doubling resolution quadruples token count, conditions apply to groups of frames rather than individual ones, and each response must wait for the rest of its multi-frame block. We present PixVid, a simple yet effective method that lifts a pretrained latent video model to directly generate every frame in pixel space. PixVid keeps the diffusion transformer and replaces the VAE decoder with a convolutional head that renders its outputs into pixels. We find that predicting clean video rather than velocity, together with a larger noise shift, is key to quality. Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B, PixVid is competitive with the latent baseline within $\sim 1.3$M training clips. Working framewise in pixels, it generates at $2\times$ higher resolution with the same per-frame token count, keeps depth-conditioned video editing aligned under fast motion, and responds to each action at the next frame. Project page: https://chenshuo20.github.io/PixVid/

items.title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding
items.summary: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.

items.title: TTB: Test-time Baking for Efficient Rendering of Decoder-only View Synthesis Models
items.summary: Decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) with KV-cache have recently achieved state-of-the-art quality by regressing novel views from neural networks without reconstructing 3D geometry, while Test-Time Training (TTT) layers save computation but sacrifice quality. We propose Test-Time Baking (TTB), a strategy that learns to bake global scene information from cross-view attention into a lightweight MLP, enabling fast and high-fidelity novel-view decoding. The first key is to repurpose the fast-weight MLP of TTT to learn the cross-view attention mapping explicitly from its input-output pairs, rather than replacing attention entirely, achieving the same rendering efficiency as TTT while delivering substantially higher quality. The second key addresses a modality misalignment between context prefilling and novel-view rendering: we disentangle context tokens into camera-only context rendering tokens to serve as TTB input, and context ground-truth tokens with image content to serve as the TTB mapping target, ensuring the baked MLPs are relieved of the modality generalization challenge between context and novel-view processing. Our method achieves up to **23x** rendering speedup with quality on par with the state-of-the-art across several benchmarks. Project page: https://test-time-baking.github.io

items.title: ArchSpace: Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing LLM Architecture Research
items.summary: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. In industry, teams such as those behind DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi routinely introduce architectural innovations, yet public reports rarely document which ideas succeeded, which were abandoned, and why. In academia, limited compute and inconsistent baselines often restrict evaluations to small-scale, single-point comparisons, making it difficult to establish whether improvements hold at larger scales or translate into broader impact. ArchSpace addresses both gaps as a public platform for Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing Architecture Researc}: each proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. To evaluate ideas before costly large-scale training, ArchSpace leverages scaling laws to predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments, a practice widely adopted in industry. We provide initial references that make the platform usable: Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe. Ideas validated through this review can in turn become new baselines, and ArchSpace thereby aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape the next generation of models.

items.title: ProtoVis-Nav: Prototypical Visual Imagination for Visual-Spatial Aligned UAV Navigation
items.summary: Vision language navigation (VLN) is very challenging for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) since small errors in 3D motion prediction can lead to navigation errors and collisions. Unable to fathom execution outcomes in 3D environments, existing methods often struggle to predict accurate navigation waypoints from language instructions. To solve this, we introduce the Prototypical Visual Imagination framework, shortened as ProtoVis-Nav, which forces the model to imagine an outcome-associated local visual representation for the intended next UAV movement. Specifically, we predict feature prototypes and use their linear combination to estimate the visual feature of the target region. In this manner, the VLN model first imagines the local visual representation of the next intended location, and then uses predicted prototypes as context for generating the final action, promoting alignment between visual context and waypoint outputs. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the ProtoVis-Nav framework and show substantial improvements over existing baselines.
